 5 Expert-Approved Lessons We Can Learn From Korean Haircare For Glossier, Glassier Hair
 K-beauty rewrote the rules of skincare—now that same thinking is transforming how we care for our hair 
 Delaney Loane

 Whether your personal obsession arrived in the form of a 12-step routine or a glass-skin fixation, Korean beauty transformed the way we treat our faces. It turned skincare into a ritual, a hobby and, for some of us, a full-blown personality trait. Because it wasn’t simply about connecting with our complexions or amassing a collection of beautiful topicals for the sake of a shelf shot. The ‘secrets’ of Korean skincare weren’t just clever marketing—they worked.
 Advertisement 
 Now, our fascination with K-beauty is moving from skin to hair. Mina Joung , Korean hair stylist at Melbourne’s AFEAT Salon , isn’t surprised. “People have already experienced how considered and innovative Korean skincare can be, so I think it’s very natural that the interest is now moving into hair and scalp care.” But Korean haircare isn’t simply skincare by another name. It brings a more holistic way of approaching hair: putting the scalp and the science before the styling, and in turn, giving every style a more polished finish.
 So how can we create said finish for ourselves? By leaning into the same approach. Here are 5 lessons we can learn from Korean haircare (and the scrubs, tonics and tools that’ll help us lock in our shiniest hair yet)…
 #1: Shine Enhances Every Style
 While trends evolve, one thing remains constant across all continents: shine is a visible marker of hair health.
 “In Korea, it’s not only about creating a beautiful hairstyle. There is a lot of emphasis on the hair itself looking soft, healthy, glossy and well maintained,” Joung explains. “With the influence of K-pop, K-dramas and Korean fashion, clients are now interested not only in Korean layers, soft curls and natural volume, but also in how to achieve the healthy, polished hair that completes those looks.”
 Advertisement 
 #2: Prevention Is Easier Than Repair
 As with Korean skincare, the philosophy is to stay ahead of the problem rather than wait for one to appear. “One of the biggest differences is that Korean haircare tends to focus on consistent maintenance and prevention, rather than waiting until the hair becomes extremely damaged and then trying to repair it,” says Joung.
 #3: Maintaining Balance Is Key
 That doesn’t necessarily mean piling on products at home. “It starts with choosing a shampoo that suits your scalp type and cleansing properly without over-stripping the skin. If there is significant oil, buildup or styling-product residue, an occasional scalp exfoliation or scrub can also be useful,” Joung clarifies.
 And if your hair already shows signs of damage, targeted care still has a place. “For damaged hair, I tend to look for a good balance of protein, amino acids, hydration, oils and conditioning ingredients rather than focusing on only one ingredient,” she shares. What that balance looks like, however, depends on the hair in question. “Hair thickness, porosity, level of damage, colour history and scalp condition all influence which treatment is going to work best,” Joung notes.
 Advertisement 
 The desired finish is simple: healthy-looking hair that still feels light and effortless. “People want hydration, softness and shine, but without making the hair feel heavy or oily. That balance is very important.”
 #4: Scalp Care Goes Beyond Just A Scrub
 In Korean haircare, healthy-looking hair starts where it grows: the scalp. We exfoliate, hydrate and treat the skin on our faces, yet the skin a few centimetres higher has traditionally been lucky to get a thorough shampoo. Scalp care has already made its way into Australian bathrooms, but the Korean approach goes beyond adding a scrub to the rotation every few washes.
 The distinction is in how specifically that care is applied. “Scalp exfoliation, scalp tonics, ampoules and scalp massage are relatively familiar concepts in Korea,” says Joung. “The scalp, roots, mid-lengths and ends can all have different needs, so rather than expecting one product to do everything, Korean haircare tends to be more targeted and layered.”
 And sometimes, scalp care is as much about what you do as what you apply. “I also think something very simple — properly drying the scalp after washing rather than leaving it damp for a long period — is an important part of scalp care,” says Joung.

 #5: The Tingling Sensation Means It’s Working
 As Korean haircare finds a growing audience in Australia, the question is how the approach will translate. “I definitely think scalp care will continue to grow in Australia. However, I think it may evolve slightly differently here compared with Korea.”
 She’s already seeing hints of that in the salon. Some Korean scalp-care products deliver a pronounced cooling or tingling effect — a cue Korean clients may associate with feeling refreshed and deeply cleansed. For Australian clients, it can be more confronting. “I’ve had some Australian clients experience a strong cooling sensation and ask whether the product is chemically exfoliating or stripping the scalp because the sensation feels quite intense to them,” Joung explains.

 Delaney began her career in the Australian beauty media industry in 2015, landing amidst the glossy world of women’s lifestyle magazines (or more literally, in their beauty cupboards). Since then, she has gone on to write across a multitude of beloved Australian media brands, including OK!, NW, InStyle, and Harper’s BAZAAR. She’s covered every side of beauty content, from directing beauty editorial shoots to rounding up the best glossy serums for golden hour skin. Having spent nearly a decade immersed in the beauty realm, Delaney’s knowledge of beauty is as extensive as her collection of tinted lip oils (read: extremely extensive). Delaney currently shares her beauty wisdom across ELLE as well as BEAUTYcrew, beautyheaven and Marie Claire.
